reference.source: ERS/ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
clinicalPearls: PAH is pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (WHO Group 1): mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg with a pulmonary artery wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less and pulmonary vascular resistance greater than 2 Wood units at right heart catheterisation.

Subtypes include idiopathic, heritable (commonly BMPR2 mutations), drug or toxin induced (for example dexfenfluramine, methamphetamine), and forms associated with connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease, portal hypertension, HIV and schistosomiasis.
Systemic sclerosis is the commonest connective tissue disease association and warrants annual screening.
Right heart catheterisation is mandatory for diagnosis; echocardiography only estimates probability and cannot confirm PAH.
Acute vasoreactivity testing identifies the minority (mainly idiopathic, heritable or drug induced) who respond to and benefit from calcium channel blockers.
Risk stratification using functional class, exercise capacity, natriuretic peptides and haemodynamics guides escalation and the intensity of therapy.

Targeted therapies act on three pathways: endothelin (endothelin receptor antagonists), nitric oxide (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators) and prostacyclin (prostacyclin analogues and receptor agonists).
Upfront combination therapy is now standard for most patients, with parenteral prostacyclins reserved for high-risk disease and transplantation for refractory cases.
reference.pathophysiology: PAH results from a progressive vasculopathy of the small pulmonary arteries driven by endothelial dysfunction, with an imbalance between vasoconstrictor and mitogenic mediators (endothelin-1, thromboxane) and vasodilator and antiproliferative mediators (nitric oxide, prostacyclin). This favours vasoconstriction, smooth muscle and endothelial proliferation, in-situ thrombosis and adventitial remodelling, producing intimal fibrosis, medial hypertrophy and plexiform lesions. Impaired bone morphogenetic protein signalling, classically through BMPR2 loss of function, promotes this angioproliferation. The resulting rise in pulmonary vascular resistance increases right ventricular afterload, leading initially to right ventricular hypertrophy and ultimately to dilatation and failure, which determines symptoms and survival.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (Group 2)
Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease or hypoxia (Group 3)
Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis
Deconditioning or other causes of exertional dyspnoea
additionalInvestigations: Right heart catheterisation with acute vasoreactivity testing
Ventilation/perfusion scan to exclude chronic thromboembolic disease
Connective tissue disease serology (ANA, anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70), HIV test and liver studies
Cardiac MRI and CT pulmonary angiography
Six-minute walk test and natriuretic peptides for risk assessment
redFlags: Exertional syncope or presyncope, a marker of severe disease
Signs of right heart failure (raised JVP, ascites, peripheral oedema)
Rapidly declining exercise capacity or functional class
reference.prognosis: Once uniformly fatal within a few years, prognosis has improved substantially with modern risk-based combination therapy. Nonetheless PAH remains a progressive, incurable disease short of lung transplantation, and outcome depends heavily on right ventricular function and treatment response.
pitfalls: Diagnosing PAH on echocardiography alone without confirmatory right heart catheterisation.
Missing an elevated wedge pressure and mislabelling Group 2 (left heart) disease as PAH.
Prescribing calcium channel blockers to non-vasoreactive patients, which can be harmful.
Failing to screen at-risk groups such as those with systemic sclerosis, BMPR2 carriers and portal hypertension.
Overlooking pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or capillary haemangiomatosis, in whom vasodilators can precipitate pulmonary oedema.
